text:
The air in the precinct was thick with the scent of stale coffee and impending change. Detective Howard stared at the file on his desk, the paper trembling slightly in his grip. Tomorrow was his last day. Thirty years of service, and he was leaving with his head held high, or so he had told himself. But the evidence before him was a jagged shard of glass in his heart.

It implicated Miller. His partner. The man who had covered for him when he was drunk on New Year’s Eve, the man who had pulled him from a burning car in '98. The crime was embezzlement, massive and systematic, funneling city funds into offshore accounts. The trail led directly to Miller’s signature.

Howard’s duty screamed at him to turn it in. The badge he wore demanded it. But his heart, the part of him that had bled for this partnership, begged him to look away. To burn the file. To let the sun rise on his retirement without the stain of betrayal.

He thought of the orange juice they used to share in the breakroom, the bright, vibrant color that always seemed to promise a fresh start. *Orange*. The fruit. The color. It was a simple thing, a coincidence of language, but now it felt like a mockery. The bright, cheerful hue of the fruit masked the bitter, acidic truth of the situation. Just as the bright promise of retirement masked the rotting core of his partner’s deceit.

If he reported it, he destroyed the only friendship that had mattered. If he didn’t, he destroyed himself. The tension coiled in his chest, tight and suffocating. He looked at the orange peel on the counter, its color vivid against the gray steel of the desk. It was a reminder of a time when things were simple, when colors were just colors and fruits were just food. Now, everything was tainted. The line between loyalty and law had blurred, leaving him stranded in a gray area where no amount of orange juice could wash away the guilt.

He picked up the file. His hand hovered over the shredder. The conflict wasn't just about right and wrong; it was about who he was when no one was watching. And as the clock ticked down to his final hour, Howard realized that the color orange, like his conscience, was not a comfort, but a warning.
